transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-04
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Moretti (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Solstice CTO), Evan Park (Head of ML), Dana Li (DevOps), Tom Keller (Product)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be rough):
Solstice is prototyping an LLM-based insights feature inside their analytics dashboard. Primary concerns: time-to-first-token for PLG experience, data residency and network (VPC / peering), and cost vs latency tradeoffs between hosted, reserved Dedicated, and Private on-prem. They requested trial credits, a short benchmark script, and security docs (SOC 2, SSO, KMS).

Topics covered:
- Quickstart / time-to-first-token (TTFT) expectations
- Free credits and sandbox account flow
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs for a mid-size analytics vendor
- Security: SSO, audit logs, KMS, data retention
- Pilot scope and success criteria

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood side, and with me is Luca from our SE team. How are you all?
[00:06] Priya Rao: Hey Maya, good thanks. Busy day but excited to dig in.
[00:09] Evan Park: Hi, thanks. We wanted to nail down the fastest path to get a prototype into the product.
[00:13] Maya Chen: Great. Quick agenda: TTFT, what you need for an eval — credits, scripts — and then VP C / private concerns. We'll leave time for questions. Is that ok?
[00:21] Tom Keller: Sounds good. We have about 45 minutes, thanks.
[00:24] Luca Moretti: Cool. So first level question — do you plan to let end users hit the hosted API directly (PLG) or will you proxy through your backend?
[00:33] Priya Rao: We'll proxy through our backend, but our product team wants the initial user trial to feel instant — so response time on the first call matters a lot. We call it TTFT — time-to-first-token.
[00:42] Evan Park: We also need embeddings for search and a small summarization lambda on the backend. Volume initially is low — maybe 50 requests a minute during a spike.
[00:50] Luca Moretti: Helpful. For TTFT the biggest contributors are cold model startup (if you're on a private dedicated instance), SDK handshake, and any VPN/NAT traversal when using Private. For Hosted we keep warm pools so the cold start impact is minimal — often sub-200ms for typical 2k token prompts in our hosted profile. But that depends on the model.
[01:10] Priya Rao: That's one of our questions: which models do you recommend for a low-latency prototype? We care about cost too.
[01:15] Maya Chen: Right. For prototyping we usually suggest one of the 8-bit quantized open models we host — good latency/cost balance. We can also snapshot a smaller variant for Dedicated. Luca can speak to exact numbers.
[01:25] Luca Moretti: Sure — for host ed small models you can expect ~80–150ms per token on RTX-like hardware for generation-only workloads. If you prefer embeddings-only flows, our smaller embedding models are cheaper and very fast (tens of ms). For Dedicated, you get predictability but you'll need reserved capacity and some scale to justify it.
[01:41] Dana Li: Quick question — network. If we use Redwood Hosted, how does traffic traverse? We have strict egress firewall rules and we run in us-east-1.
[01:50] Maya Chen: Good — Hosted runs in major cloud regions; we can use private peering or a VPC peering arrangement for Dedicated/Private. For Hosted we support VPC endpoints and IP allowlists, but if you need full isolation, Private (VPC-managed or on-prem bundle) is the path.
[02:02] Tom Keller: Is the quickstart for Hosted self-serve? Team wants to try with minimal infra work.
[02:06] Maya Chen: Yes — PLG flow is self-serve. We'll send trial credits and a one-click sandbox that includes SDK snippets, a tiny sample app, and a curl example for TTFT checks.
[02:13] Evan Park: Nice. What does the first request latency look like for unauthenticated sample calls from a dev laptop?
[02:18] Luca Moretti: From a dev laptop, if you use the Hosted sandbox it is usually under a second — often 400–800ms to first token for short prompts. But again, that varies with model and network. We'll include a script so you can measure from your network.
[02:29] [crosstalk — overlapping voices]
[02:31] Priya Rao: Two more layers — security certs and compliance. We need SOC 2 Type II and SSO via SAML. Also audit logs for PII access.
[02:41] Maya Chen: Understood. We have SOC 2 material and an SSO/SAML integration guide. We also provide token-level logs and an A P I usage history for audit. For Private we can route logs to your SIEM if you prefer.
[02:52] Dana Li: KMS — we use a customer-managed KMS. Can Redwood integrate with that?
[02:56] Luca Moretti: Yes, for Private we support bringing your own KMS/HSM; for Dedicated we can integrate with customer KMS via IAM roles and encrypted volumes. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption and a key-rotation cadence; if you require CMKs we can discuss a managed key option.
[03:12] Tom Keller: Good. Let's talk about cost — early stage we want low friction but not runaway spend. If we start on Hosted, what's the path to Dedicated or Private?
[03:22] Maya Chen: Customers typically start on Hosted for fast TTFT and PLG experiments. When predictable traffic or compliance needs arise, we propose Dedicated with reserved GPU pools — that gives you predictable unit cost and SLOs. Private is for strict data residency or air-gapped needs. We can show a cost model; I will include a rough cost spreadsheet in the follow-up.
[03:40] Evan Park: What's the typical lead time to move from Hosted to Dedicated? We have a launch target in Q4.
[03:46] Luca Moretti: For Dedicated the procurement and capacity setup is usually 4–8 weeks depending on region and instance sizes. Private on-prem can be longer — often 8–16 weeks including validation and network setup. But for an initial pilot you can stay Hosted and then contract Dedicated capacity when it makes sense.
[03:58] Priya Rao: Okay that timeline could work. For our pilot success criteria we want: sub-500ms median response for the summarization API, embedding recall above baseline on our dataset, and no PII retention in logs.
[04:12] Maya Chen: Perfect, we'll make those explicit in the pilot definition. Luca — any notes on how we instrument recall/evals?
[04:17] Luca Moretti: Yes — we provide eval harnesses and you can attach prompt sets. We also have quality regression alerts tied to those prompt sets so you can detect drift after model or quant changes. For embeddings recall we can run a batch of queries and compute nearest-neighbor recall against your labeled set.
[04:31] Dana Li: On the networking side, if you do peering, our infra team needs the IP ranges and NAT expectations. We also have a carrier NAT that changes egress IPs — that's a pain for allowlists.
[04:42] Maya Chen: Noted. We can also use a VPC endpoint or private link in us-east-1 to avoid changing egress IPs. We'll include network artifacts in the security pack.
[04:52] Tom Keller: You mentioned rollouts and graceful fallback — how does Redwood handle model fallbacks if a new model regresses?
[04:58] Luca Moretti: We support canary rollouts and traffic split policies at the model/version level. We also have automatic fallback to a stable variant if latency or error rates spike. These are configurable per-route.
[05:10] Priya Rao: Does that require code changes or is it config in the console?
[05:14] Luca Moretti: Mostly config. You can route traffic by percent, set SLO gates, and define fallback model mappings. SDKs can also opt in to features but the heavy lifting is in the Console/API.
[05:23] [silence for a few seconds]
[05:30] Priya Rao: Two more things: data residency — we need EU data to remain in eu-west-1 for some customers. And encryption-in-transit requirements.
[05:39] Maya Chen: We have region pinning; in Hosted we can pin workloads to eu-west-1 and ensure storage is regional. TLS in transit is standard; if you need mTLS we can discuss a Private path.
[05:49] Evan Park: Onboarding — who do we loop in for the pilot? Our list: product owner (Tom), ML lead (Evan), infra (Dana) and maybe a security reviewer (Priya).
[05:58] Maya Chen: Great. For the pilot SE involvement will be Luca. I'll include contacts and propose a kickoff time for week of Aug 16.
[06:04] Tom Keller: Ok. Walk me through the quickstart steps so we can estimate dev time.
[06:09] Luca Moretti: Step 1: You sign up and accept the trial credits. Step 2: grab the API key in the sandbox. Step 3: run the sample app — we've got a node and python example that does embedding + summarization. Step 4: run the mini-benchmark which will exercise 100 sample requests and measure latencies and token costs. Step 5: decide whether you want Dedicated trial or continue on Hosted. For most teams the initial dev time is a couple hours to get a request flowing.
[06:32] Priya Rao: Couple hours sounds doable. Any gotchas?
[06:35] Luca Moretti: If you are behind strict corporate proxies, that can add auth friction. Also, if you want to test a very long context or very large batch embeddings, we recommend running the benchmark from an internal VM to avoid laptop network variance.
[06:47] Dana Li: On IAM — do you create a per-service key or per-developer keys? We prefer per-service keys and short TTLs.
[06:54] Maya Chen: Best practice is per-service key and rotate them; we support short TTLs and key rotation via the Console. We'll include recommended policies in the quickstart docs.
[07:03] [background noise — paper rustling]
[07:08] Priya Rao: One last technical nit: we use a vector store internally. Do you have guides for chunking and embedding choices? We want to avoid huge embedding costs.
[07:19] Luca Moretti: Yes, we have recommendations: 1) chunk by semantic boundaries, 2) limit chunk size to target model's sweet spot (~512–1k tokens), 3) use quantized embeddings where acceptable to save cost. We'll send a short note with examples.
[07:33] Tom Keller: Who else do we need to convince internally? Legal will want a data processing addendum and security will want details on audit logs and retention.
[07:41] Maya Chen: I'll attach our DPA and SOC 2 report in the follow-up. For audit logs we can supply both Console exports and an audit stream for SIEM integration on Private/Dedicated.
[07:52] Evan Park: Great. On the metrics side, what observability will we get during the pilot?
[07:57] Luca Moretti: You'll get per-route latency percentiles, token-level cost breakdown, error traces, and per-token provenance metadata (best-effort) for debugging. We'll show you a dashboard and can instrument additional traces if you need them.
[08:10] Priya Rao: If we hit production scale in Q4, what's the pricing model? Committed monthly for Dedicated?
[08:16] Maya Chen: Yes — Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly/annual commits. Hosted remains usage-based. We'll include a few scenario-based TCO examples in the follow-up.
[08:26] [short pause]
[08:30] Tom Keller: Ok, let's capture the immediate asks so we don't lose them.
[08:33] Maya Chen: Sure — immediate asks: credits + quickstart, benchmark script, security pack (SOC2, DPA, SSO guide), network IP ranges, and suggested models/costs. Anything else?
[08:44] Priya Rao: Also a proposed pilot success doc with the three KPIs we mentioned.
[08:48] Maya Chen: Got it. We'll send all that. Luca, any final technical caveats?
[08:53] Luca Moretti: Just that for TTFT measurement please use the supplied script and run it from your dev environment and from an internal VM to compare. Also, if you want to simulate spikes, we can help run a short performance run.
[09:06] Dana Li: Good, thanks. We'll get the infra doc to you.
[09:10] Maya Chen: Great. Next steps recap: I'll send credits and materials tomorrow; Luca will send the benchmark by next week; Dana will provide infra diagrams. We'll lock a pilot kickoff for week of Aug 16.
[09:20] Tom Keller: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[09:22] Priya Rao: Thanks.
[09:24] Maya Chen: Thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.
